title: Preconception Care: Optimize Before Pregnancy Starts
bottomLine: Preconception care identifies modifiable medication, chronic disease, immunization, infection, genetic and social risks before pregnancy. If pregnancy is not desired now, effective contraception is part of disease optimization.
recognize: Diabetes, hypertension, epilepsy, obesity, thyroid disease, mental illness and teratogenic medications may need adjustment before conception.
differentiate: Pregnancy intention can change; do not assume desire or non-desire for pregnancy based on age, relationship or parity.
assessment: Ask pregnancy goals, contraception, folate, medications/supplements, chronic disease control, vaccines, substance use, infection risk, genetics/family history and social safety.
workup: Order disease- and risk-specific tests rather than a universal preconception panel.
management: Optimize chronic disease, review teratogenic medications, update indicated immunizations, recommend folic acid based on risk and arrange specialty consultation for complex disease.
medicationSafety: Do not stop essential medication abruptly; switch to safer effective alternatives through shared planning when possible.
counselling: Use reproductive life-plan questions without coercion.
followUp: Confirm medication and disease targets before attempting conception when feasible.
examTrap: Telling a patient to stop an effective high-risk medication immediately without considering disease destabilization or an alternative plan.
oneLinePearl: Preconception care is preventive medicine before the pregnancy test turns positive.

title: Routine Prenatal Care: Date, Screen, Prevent, Reassess Risk
bottomLine: Prenatal care establishes gestational age, baseline maternal risk, fetal screening choices, infection and blood-group status, immunization and prevention needs, then repeatedly reassesses maternal and fetal wellbeing as pregnancy evolves.
recognize: Pregnancy risk can change with hypertension, diabetes, bleeding, growth concerns, mental health, substance use or social instability.
differentiate: Screening estimates risk; a positive prenatal screen is not a definitive fetal diagnosis.
assessment: Confirm dating/LMP, obstetric history, chronic disease, medications, blood group, infection/immunization, genetic history, nutrition, mental health, substance use and social safety.
workup: Use Canadian/provincial prenatal laboratory and aneuploidy screening pathways with informed choice; anatomy ultrasound and later testing follow gestational age and risk.
management: Provide indicated folate, vaccines, aspirin prophylaxis for appropriate preeclampsia risk, Rh immune globulin according to blood group/events, and specialty referral when risk increases.
medicationSafety: Pregnancy medication decisions should compare fetal exposure risk with the risk of undertreated maternal disease.
redFlags: Reduced fetal movement later in pregnancy
counselling: Use informed choice for prenatal screening and avoid presenting optional testing as mandatory.
followUp: Document gestational milestones, outstanding results and clear ownership for abnormal screens.
examTrap: Treating a positive screening result as a confirmed diagnosis without offering diagnostic counselling/testing.
oneLinePearl: Prenatal screening changes probability; diagnostic testing answers the diagnosis question.

title: Gestational Diabetes: Control Glucose Without Missing Postpartum Diabetes Risk
bottomLine: Gestational diabetes is screened and diagnosed using pregnancy-specific criteria, treated to reduce maternal and fetal complications, and followed postpartum because future type 2 diabetes risk remains high even after glucose normalizes.
recognize: Risk factors include prior GDM, macrosomia, obesity, family history and some higher-risk ethnocultural populations, but universal or broad screening is common depending on Canadian pathway.
differentiate: Overt pre-existing diabetes first recognized in pregnancy has different severity and follow-up implications.
assessment: Assess gestational age, glucose results, fetal growth, diet/access, prior GDM, medications and hypertension.
workup: Use current Canadian pregnancy glucose-screening criteria; monitor fetal growth and maternal glucose according to severity.
management: Use nutrition/activity support and insulin when pharmacologic treatment is needed in many Canadian pathways; specialist care for poor control or complications.
medicationSafety: Medication choices in pregnancy require current obstetric/diabetes guidance; postpartum insulin needs can fall rapidly.
counselling: Explain that GDM is not caused by personal failure and that postpartum prevention matters.
followUp: Arrange postpartum glucose testing and ongoing diabetes screening.
examTrap: Discharging after delivery with no postpartum diabetes testing because glucose normalized in hospital.
oneLinePearl: GDM ends with delivery physiologically, but its diabetes risk does not.

title: Hypertension in Pregnancy: Preeclampsia Is Multisystem Disease
bottomLine: Preeclampsia is not defined by edema and can occur with severe end-organ features even when proteinuria is absent. Severe hypertension, neurologic symptoms, pulmonary edema, hepatic/hematologic dysfunction or fetal compromise require urgent obstetric assessment.
recognize: New hypertension after 20 weeks with proteinuria or maternal organ dysfunction supports preeclampsia; postpartum disease can occur after delivery.
differentiate: Chronic hypertension predates pregnancy or occurs early; gestational hypertension lacks preeclampsia features at diagnosis but can progress.
assessment: Assess BP correctly, headache/vision, RUQ/epigastric pain, dyspnea, edema/weight change, fetal movement and prior risk.
workup: Use CBC/platelets, creatinine, AST/ALT, urine protein assessment and fetal surveillance according to severity.
management: Severe-range hypertension requires urgent treatment; magnesium sulfate is used for seizure prevention/treatment in appropriate severe preeclampsia/eclampsia; delivery timing depends on maternal/fetal status and gestation.
medicationSafety: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated during pregnancy; postpartum antihypertensive choices differ and breastfeeding considerations matter.
counselling: Teach postpartum warning signs because preeclampsia can worsen or first appear after delivery.
followUp: Ensure postpartum BP and long-term cardiovascular risk follow-up.
examTrap: Ruling out preeclampsia because the urine protein test is negative despite severe hypertension and neurologic symptoms.
oneLinePearl: Preeclampsia is a multisystem diagnosis, not a proteinuria diagnosis.
sourceBasis: SOGC hypertensive disorders of pregnancy guidance

title: Hyperemesis Gravidarum: Vomiting Becomes a Metabolic Problem
bottomLine: Nausea and vomiting are common in pregnancy, but inability to maintain hydration, significant weight loss, electrolyte abnormalities or ketotic illness requires active treatment and alternative-diagnosis review.
recognize: Persistent vomiting with dehydration, weight loss and functional impairment suggests hyperemesis.
differentiate: Molar pregnancy, multiple gestation, thyroid disease, hepatitis, pancreatitis, appendicitis and infection can cause disproportionate vomiting.
assessment: Assess weight trajectory, hydration, urine output, abdominal pain, fever, headache, medications and gestational context.
workup: Use electrolytes, renal/liver tests, urine and ultrasound when severity or alternate diagnoses warrant.
management: Use oral/IV hydration, thiamine when prolonged poor intake, and pregnancy-appropriate antiemetics; admit refractory or metabolically unstable patients.
medicationSafety: Give thiamine before substantial dextrose in prolonged malnutrition risk to reduce Wernicke risk.
counselling: Validate symptom burden and provide a stepped medication plan.
followUp: Track weight, hydration and medication response.
examTrap: Giving large dextrose loads to a severely malnourished vomiting patient before addressing thiamine deficiency risk.
oneLinePearl: Hyperemesis is not just nausea—it is hydration, nutrition and electrolyte disease.
sourceBasis: SOGC pregnancy nausea and vomiting practice resources

title: Preterm Labour and PPROM: Gestational Age Changes Everything
bottomLine: Regular contractions with cervical change before term or rupture of membranes before labour requires gestational-age-specific obstetric care. Infection, fetal status and imminent delivery determine urgency and treatment.
recognize: Fluid leakage, pelvic pressure, contractions, bleeding or back pain can be presenting symptoms.
differentiate: Physiologic contractions lack progressive cervical change; urinary discharge and semen can mimic membrane rupture.
assessment: Assess gestational age, contraction pattern, fluid, bleeding, fever, fetal movement and prior preterm birth.
workup: Use sterile speculum testing for membrane rupture and fetal/cervical assessment through the obstetric pathway; avoid digital cervical examination when PPROM is suspected unless delivery is imminent and it is clinically required.
management: Transfer to obstetric care; use antenatal corticosteroids, magnesium for fetal neuroprotection, latency antibiotics or tocolysis only in indicated gestational and clinical contexts.
medicationSafety: Tocolysis is not appropriate in situations where delivery is safer, such as significant infection or fetal/maternal instability.
counselling: Explain why treatment depends heavily on gestational age and infection/fetal status.
followUp: Coordinate neonatal and maternal care after preterm birth or PPROM.
examTrap: Performing repeated digital cervical examinations after suspected PPROM and increasing infection risk.
oneLinePearl: PPROM is diagnosed with minimal contamination and managed by gestational age plus infection/fetal status.
sourceBasis: SOGC preterm labour and PPROM guidance

title: Labour Triage: True Labour, Bleeding, Rupture, or Fetal Concern?
bottomLine: Late-pregnancy triage must quickly identify fetal compromise, significant bleeding, ruptured membranes, hypertensive disease and active labour. Reassuring the parent without assessing fetal wellbeing can miss the highest-risk problem.
recognize: True labour causes regular painful contractions with cervical change; rupture may present as a gush or persistent leaking.
differentiate: Placental abruption can be concealed; placenta previa classically causes painless bleeding but diagnosis depends on placental location.
assessment: Assess gestational age, fetal movement, contractions, bleeding, fluid leakage, BP/symptoms and fetal heart status.
workup: Use obstetric examination and fetal monitoring matched to gestational age and symptoms; ultrasound supports placental/fetal assessment.
management: Escalate decreased fetal movement, abnormal fetal heart tracing, significant bleeding, hypertensive emergency or cord prolapse immediately.
medicationSafety: Do not perform digital vaginal examination in significant antepartum bleeding until placenta previa has been excluded when clinically relevant.
counselling: Give clear return instructions if early labour is managed at home.
followUp: Document fetal assessment and disposition clearly.
examTrap: Performing a digital vaginal examination in painless third-trimester bleeding before placental location is known.
oneLinePearl: Third-trimester bleeding is a placenta question before it is a cervix question.

title: Postpartum Hemorrhage: Tone, Trauma, Tissue, Thrombin
bottomLine: Postpartum hemorrhage is treated simultaneously with resuscitation and cause control. Use the four Ts—tone, trauma, tissue and thrombin—to drive intervention while activating the hemorrhage pathway early.
recognize: Uterine atony is the most common cause, but retained placenta, laceration, inversion and coagulopathy require different treatment.
differentiate: Visible blood loss can underestimate severity; tachycardia, hypotension and altered perfusion signal physiologic impact.
assessment: Assess uterine tone, placental completeness, genital tract trauma, vitals, IV access and ongoing quantified blood loss.
workup: CBC/coagulation/fibrinogen and blood bank testing are obtained while treatment proceeds.
management: Massage atonic uterus, use uterotonics according to contraindications, give tranexamic acid within the evidence-based window when indicated, replace blood products and escalate to procedural/surgical control.
medicationSafety: Methylergonovine is problematic in severe hypertension; carboprost is problematic in asthma—choose uterotonics with comorbidity in mind.
counselling: After stabilization, discuss anemia, recurrence risk and emotional impact.
followUp: Ensure postpartum hemoglobin/iron and mental-health recovery are addressed.
examTrap: Giving the same uterotonic to every hemorrhage patient without checking asthma or hypertension contraindications.
oneLinePearl: PPH management is resuscitation plus the four Ts, in parallel.
sourceBasis: SOGC postpartum hemorrhage resources and ALARM principles

title: Postpartum Fever: Endometritis, Wound, Breast, Urine, or Clot?
bottomLine: Postpartum fever needs a source. Uterine tenderness and foul lochia after cesarean or prolonged labour suggest endometritis, but wound infection, mastitis, UTI/pyelonephritis, retained products and VTE must remain in the differential.
recognize: Cesarean birth is a major endometritis risk factor.
differentiate: Breast engorgement alone may cause discomfort but high fever and focal erythema suggest mastitis; unilateral leg symptoms raise VTE concern.
assessment: Assess vitals, uterine tenderness, lochia, incision/perineum, breasts, urinary symptoms and leg/chest symptoms.
workup: Use CBC, urine/cultures and ultrasound only when clinically indicated; uncomplicated endometritis is often a clinical diagnosis.
management: Use broad-spectrum antibiotics with anaerobic coverage for clinically significant postpartum endometritis and escalate sepsis/retained-products concerns.
medicationSafety: Antibiotic choice should account for allergy, breastfeeding and local resistance.
counselling: Teach that postpartum infection symptoms warrant prompt assessment rather than waiting for the routine six-week visit.
followUp: Confirm fever and uterine tenderness resolve.
examTrap: Attributing postpartum fever automatically to breast engorgement without examining the uterus and wound.
oneLinePearl: Postpartum fever is a source-finding problem.

title: Lactational Mastitis: Support Milk Removal Without Over-Treating Inflammation
bottomLine: Lactational breast inflammation exists on a spectrum from ductal narrowing to bacterial mastitis and abscess. Continue physiologic feeding or milk removal as tolerated, avoid aggressive breast massage and reserve antibiotics for bacterial features.
recognize: Focal breast pain/erythema with systemic symptoms can represent bacterial mastitis; persistent fluctuant mass suggests abscess.
differentiate: Engorgement and inflammatory mastitis can improve without antibiotics; inflammatory breast cancer is a rare but important persistent mimic.
assessment: Assess fever, focal mass, nipple trauma, oversupply/pumping pattern, feeding technique and duration of symptoms.
workup: Ultrasound is used when abscess is suspected or symptoms fail to improve; culture selected recurrent/severe cases.
management: Use anti-inflammatory measures, normal feeding, lactation support and targeted antibiotics when bacterial mastitis is likely; drain abscess.
medicationSafety: Avoid excessive pumping to 'empty' the breast, which can worsen hyperlactation and inflammation.
redFlags: Persistent inflammatory changes despite appropriate therapy
counselling: Breastfeeding can usually continue and is not harmful to the infant in uncomplicated mastitis.
followUp: Reassess non-resolving focal inflammation to exclude abscess or other breast disease.
examTrap: Telling a lactating patient to aggressively massage and completely empty the breast after every feed.
oneLinePearl: Mastitis care is gentle milk physiology, not forceful emptying.

title: Vaginitis: Discharge Is a Differential, Not a Diagnosis
bottomLine: Vaginal discharge or irritation can reflect bacterial vaginosis, candidiasis, trichomoniasis, cervicitis, atrophy, dermatitis or retained foreign body. Symptoms alone are often insufficient to distinguish them.
recognize: BV often causes thin malodorous discharge; candidiasis often causes pruritus and thick discharge; trichomoniasis is an STI with variable discharge.
differentiate: Cervical motion/pelvic tenderness raises PID; postmenopausal dryness and dyspareunia may be genitourinary syndrome of menopause.
assessment: Ask pregnancy, STI risk, antibiotics, diabetes, recurrent symptoms, odor/pruritus/pain and irritant exposures; perform exam/testing when diagnosis is uncertain.
workup: Use vaginal pH, microscopy/NAAT or other validated testing according to syndrome and local access.
management: Treat the confirmed or strongly supported cause; partner treatment is organism-specific rather than universal.
medicationSafety: Repeated empiric antifungal treatment can delay diagnosis of dermatitis, BV or STI.
counselling: Use inclusive sexual history and explain which conditions are sexually transmitted and which are not.
followUp: Recurrent or refractory symptoms need diagnostic confirmation.
examTrap: Treating every pruritic discharge as yeast without considering BV, STI or dermatitis.
oneLinePearl: Vaginitis treatment starts by naming the cause.

title: Endometriosis: Cyclic Pain Is a Clinical Clue
bottomLine: Endometriosis causes cyclic or chronic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia and infertility. Treatment can begin from a strong clinical diagnosis; normal ultrasound does not exclude superficial disease.
recognize: Pain beginning before or with menses, deep dyspareunia, painful defecation and infertility are common.
differentiate: Adenomyosis, fibroids, IBS, bladder pain syndrome and pelvic-floor pain can mimic or coexist.
assessment: Assess pain timing, bleeding, sexual/bowel/bladder symptoms, fertility goals and impact on school/work.
workup: Pelvic ultrasound evaluates endometrioma/deep disease and other pathology; laparoscopy is not mandatory before all empiric treatment.
management: Use NSAIDs and hormonal suppression when appropriate; refer for refractory pain, infertility, mass or deep organ involvement.
medicationSafety: Hormonal choices require VTE, migraine, smoking and pregnancy-goal review.
counselling: Validate pain and discuss fertility without assuming pregnancy is desired.
followUp: Track function and response; persistent pain may require multidisciplinary pelvic-pain care.
examTrap: Ruling out endometriosis because a routine pelvic ultrasound is normal.
oneLinePearl: A normal ultrasound does not erase a classic endometriosis history.

title: Uterine Fibroids: Symptoms and Reproductive Goals Drive Treatment
bottomLine: Fibroids are common benign uterine tumours; treatment is based on heavy bleeding, bulk symptoms, anemia, pain and fertility goals rather than imaging size alone.
recognize: Heavy menstrual bleeding, pelvic pressure, urinary frequency and infertility can occur.
differentiate: Adenomyosis, endometrial pathology and pregnancy must be considered in abnormal bleeding.
assessment: Assess bleeding quantity, anemia symptoms, pressure/pain, fertility goals and pregnancy possibility.
workup: CBC and pelvic ultrasound are common; endometrial sampling depends on age and bleeding risk factors, not on fibroids alone.
management: Use medical bleeding control, hormonal or nonhormonal options, uterine-sparing procedures or surgery according to symptoms and reproductive goals.
medicationSafety: Estrogen-containing therapy requires standard VTE and contraindication review.
counselling: Explain that many fibroids need no treatment if asymptomatic.
followUp: Monitor symptoms and anemia rather than serial imaging of stable asymptomatic fibroids.
examTrap: Recommending hysterectomy simply because an ultrasound shows multiple fibroids.
oneLinePearl: Treat the fibroid symptoms and goals, not the scan.

title: Adnexal Mass and Torsion: Sudden Pain Is a Surgical Signal
bottomLine: Sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain with nausea, especially with an ovarian mass or pregnancy, is ovarian torsion until excluded. Doppler flow can be present despite torsion, so reassuring flow does not overrule a strong clinical picture.
recognize: Torsion pain may be intermittent as the ovary twists and untwists.
differentiate: Ectopic pregnancy, appendicitis, renal colic and ruptured cyst are important alternatives.
assessment: Assess pregnancy, onset, nausea/vomiting, bleeding, prior cyst/torsion and peritoneal signs.
workup: Pregnancy test and pelvic ultrasound are central, but urgent gynecologic consultation is warranted when clinical suspicion remains high.
management: Suspected torsion requires urgent surgical evaluation to preserve ovarian function; stable simple cysts are managed according to size, age and morphology.
medicationSafety: Analgesia should not be withheld while arranging surgical assessment.
counselling: Explain that torsion can be intermittent and imaging is not perfectly exclusionary.
examTrap: Ruling out torsion solely because Doppler ultrasound shows arterial flow.
oneLinePearl: Normal Doppler flow does not fully exclude ovarian torsion.
sourceBasis: SOGC adnexal mass and acute gynecology practice resources

title: Cervical Screening: Program Screening Is Not Symptom Evaluation
bottomLine: Cervical screening is for asymptomatic eligible people and increasingly uses HPV-based strategies across Canadian jurisdictions. Postcoital bleeding, visible cervical lesions or other symptoms require diagnostic evaluation regardless of routine screening interval.
recognize: Screening eligibility and intervals vary by province/territory and are evolving with HPV primary screening.
differentiate: A screening result estimates precancer risk; diagnostic colposcopy/biopsy confirms disease.
assessment: Confirm cervix status, prior abnormal results/treatment, immunocompromise, age and symptoms; use inclusive language for trans and nonbinary patients with a cervix.
workup: Follow the current provincial or territorial HPV/cytology pathway and colposcopy thresholds.
management: Ensure abnormal results are tracked to completion; symptomatic patients follow diagnostic rather than routine screening algorithms.
medicationSafety: Not applicable; avoid unnecessary antibiotics for contact bleeding without infection evidence.
redFlags: Loss to follow-up after high-risk result
counselling: Explain HPV natural history and that a positive HPV test does not establish cancer or infidelity.
examTrap: Telling a symptomatic patient to wait until the next scheduled screening test because their last screen was normal.
oneLinePearl: Screening schedules do not replace diagnostic evaluation of symptoms.
sourceBasis: provincial and territorial cervical screening programs

title: Infertility and Recurrent Pregnancy Loss: Evaluate Both Partners and the Pattern
bottomLine: Infertility assessment should consider ovulation, ovarian reserve context, tubal or uterine factors and semen simultaneously. Recurrent pregnancy loss warrants a structured, trauma-informed evaluation rather than blame or unsupported empiric treatment.
recognize: Age, cycle pattern, endometriosis, prior pelvic infection, surgery and male-factor infertility influence probability.
differentiate: Infertility and recurrent pregnancy loss are different syndromes and need different evaluations.
assessment: Assess duration of trying, age, cycles, pregnancy history, pelvic/STI history, sexual function, medications/substances and semen factors.
workup: Use ovulation assessment, semen analysis, uterine/tubal evaluation and targeted endocrine/genetic testing based on phenotype; SOGC updated recurrent pregnancy loss guidance in 2025.
management: Refer earlier when age, amenorrhea, severe endometriosis, tubal disease or male-factor risk makes delay harmful; manage recurrent loss according to identified cause.
medicationSafety: Avoid empiric anticoagulation, progesterone or immunologic therapies unless supported by the specific recurrent-loss context.
counselling: Use trauma-informed language and avoid implying that ordinary activity or stress caused pregnancy loss.
followUp: Coordinate fertility/genetics/obstetric services based on findings and goals.
examTrap: Completing an extensive workup of only the female partner while never ordering a semen analysis.
oneLinePearl: Infertility is a couple or gamete-source problem until proven otherwise.
